EXCESS BUSINESS LOSS CALCULATOR · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

How much of your business loss is deductible this year?

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the excess business loss limitation permanent — and, unlike most OBBBA changes, its 2026 threshold is actually LOWER than 2025's. A pass-through owner's net business loss above the threshold does not disappear; it becomes a net operating loss carried into next year instead. This tool runs the numbers for your filing status and year.

Nothing is uploaded. Your numbers are read in this browser and never leave your device — see the privacy note in the footer.

1. Filing status and tax year

Married filing jointly gets exactly double the other three statuses' shared threshold.

2. Your business numbers

Aggregate across all your trades or businesses. Wages, interest, dividends, and capital gains outside a business do not belong here — they are what the allowed loss then offsets.

Fill in your filing status, year, and business numbers, then click Calculate.

Result

What this does not cover

  • Not a full tax return. This computes one limitation on one net figure — not total tax liability, other deductions or credits, or state tax.
  • Does not compute your net business loss for you. You supply aggregate business income and deductions directly; this tool does not derive them from a Schedule C, K-1, or other source document.
  • No QBI-deduction interaction. A large business loss can reduce a future year's Section 199A qualified business income deduction — flagged, not computed. See the QBI deduction calculator.
  • No NOL carryforward valuation. The excess is flagged as an NOL carryforward, but its value in a future year (including the 80%-of-taxable-income limit) is left to a tax professional.

Common questions

What is the excess business loss limitation?

IRC Section 461(l) limits how much of a noncorporate taxpayer's net business loss can offset OTHER income — wages, interest, dividends — in the current year. It was scheduled to expire after 2028; the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made it permanent starting with the 2025 tax year.

What happens to the loss above the threshold?

It is not lost — the excess is added to your net operating loss (NOL) carryforward to next year, where it can offset up to 80% of that year's taxable income under current law, with no carryback for most businesses.

Why is the 2026 threshold LOWER than 2025's?

OBBBA rebased how this threshold is indexed for inflation, resetting it closer to its original 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act base instead of continuing to compound. The result is counterintuitive: $313,000 single/HOH/MFS in 2025 falls to $256,000 in 2026; $626,000 MFJ falls to $512,000. Most OBBBA changes raise a threshold — this one is a rare exception.

Does married filing jointly get double the single threshold?

Yes, exactly double. Single, head-of-household, and married-filing-separately filers all share the same threshold; married filing jointly gets precisely twice that figure, not a separate number of its own.

What counts as the net business loss?

Aggregate income or gain from all your trades or businesses, minus aggregate deductions attributable to those same trades or businesses. Wages, interest, dividends, and capital gains outside a business are not part of this figure — they are what the ALLOWED loss then offsets.

Is this tax advice?

No. This calculator applies the published federal excess-business-loss threshold to the numbers you enter. It does not compute your business income or deductions, model the interaction with the QBI deduction, or verify your filing status, and it is not a substitute for reviewing IRS guidance or consulting a qualified tax professional before you file.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record — nothing you enter is saved anywhere by this tool.

Everything runs in your browser. Your numbers are never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors. Anonymous feature events (estimate_calculated, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage on your device. The counts can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Also want to check your QBI deduction? See the QBI deduction calculator — a large business loss this tool flags can reduce that deduction in a future year. Selling qualified small business stock instead of running a loss? See the QSBS exclusion calculator — another OBBBA change made permanent in 2025, this one on capital gains rather than ordinary losses.

Own a short-term rental that throws off a big first-year depreciation loss? See the STR tax loophole calculator — it checks whether that loss is non-passive and how much of it clears this limit.

Working this out by hand instead? See where a hand estimate of the excess business loss limitation usually goes wrong.

Free and open source. If this helped, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This calculator vs. working out the excess business loss limitation by hand

The arithmetic looks simple — a loss compared against a threshold. The part that goes wrong by hand is which year's threshold, and what counts toward the loss in the first place.

Where a hand estimate usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake by handWhat this calculator does
2026 threshold directionAssumes the 2026 figure rose from 2025's, like almost every other inflation-indexed tax number.Uses the correct, lower 2026 figures ($256,000/$512,000 vs. 2025's $313,000/$626,000) and flags the reversal explicitly.
What counts as the lossIncludes wages, interest, or dividends in the net business loss figure.Compares only trade-or-business income and deductions against the threshold; other income is what the allowed loss then offsets.
Filing-status figureGuesses at the married-filing-jointly amount instead of using the statutory figure.Uses the exact doubled MFJ threshold from the statute for the selected year.
What happens to the excessTreats a disallowed loss as simply lost.Flags it as a net operating loss carryforward, usable against up to 80% of a future year's taxable income.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The calculator runs entirely in your browser; nothing is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the single most common mistake working this out by hand?

Assuming the 2026 threshold rose from 2025's, the way almost every other inflation-indexed tax figure does. It actually fell — from $313,000 to $256,000 single/HOH/MFS, and $626,000 to $512,000 MFJ — because OBBBA rebased the indexing formula.

What's the second most common mistake?

Including wages, interest, dividends, or capital gains in the net business loss figure. Only aggregate income and deductions from your trades or businesses count toward the threshold comparison — other income is what the ALLOWED loss then offsets, not part of the loss itself.

What arithmetic mistake gets made most often?

Assuming a joint return doubles automatically without checking — it does, but only because married filing jointly is a genuinely separate, higher figure in the statute, not a rule applied uniformly to every tax threshold. Getting the actual dollar amount wrong for the wrong reason still produces a wrong number.

What planning mistake gets made most often?

Treating a disallowed loss as gone rather than carried forward. The excess above the threshold becomes a net operating loss carryforward, usable against up to 80% of a future year's taxable income — not a permanently lost deduction, but also not immediately as valuable as it would have been this year.

Does this calculator know my complete tax situation?

No. Neither this calculator nor a by-hand worksheet built from this page computes your business income or deductions, models the QBI-deduction interaction, or values a future NOL carryforward. Both apply the same published federal threshold to the numbers you enter; verify against IRS guidance or a qualified tax professional before relying on either.

No warranty. This page and the linked calculator apply published federal excess-business-loss rules to numbers you supply. It is not legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified tax professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, and for confirming your own numbers before filing a return. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The calculator this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.
